Women and girls received an appropriate response to their needs such as psychosocial support services which included individual and group counselling, bread making and art craft activities at the WGFS. To ensure quality response services, CARE mentored the frontline staff such as the case workers and the PSS workers so they can provide individual and group counseling sessions, addressing trauma and promoting mental well-being. There were regular sessions conducted to disseminate critical information on GBV prevention and response, sexual and reproductive health, psychosocial support, and legal services. This included guidance on accessing humanitarian services, understanding legal rights, and childcare support. Additionally, the protection team had been conducting community meetings to raise awareness about GBV, aiming to transform harmful social norms and promote gender equality. As such, the WGFS provided a haven for women and girls, offering much-needed psychosocial support and counseling. This contributed significantly to their mental health and overall well-being. The ongoing skills-building programs equipped women and girls with practical skills such as bread making, bed sheets, beads making among other, fostering a sense of empowerment and resilience. This not only improved their economic prospects but also boosted their confidence and independence. The WGFs serve as a community protection network which played a crucial role in mitigating GBV risks, creating a supportive environment where survivors felt safe and protected. "

On the side of women, the project participants raised their voices that active and meaningful participation of women and girls at family and community level is very low due to male domination. However, Community said through continuous awareness campaign being conducted will ensure the barriers that prevent women and girls from leading and participating in decision-making processes, from the family and community shall come to end one day. CARE established 6 groups of EMBs in the three locations of Verteth, Akilo and Gumuruk Payam. Each group comprised on 30 individuals, equally divided into boys and men. The EMB approach engages male (men and boys) to challenge gender inequality to shift beliefs, behaviours and practices at household and community levels in support of gender equality and the empowerment of women and girls. Some of the topics covered included gender and power, sexuality, fatherhood, violence, making change, taking action among others. During the EMB sessions, men and boys have been encouraged to abandon harmful stereotypes that discriminate against women and embrace respectful, healthy relationships. They were also encouraged to support the human rights of all people in their community. The EMB approach recognizes that men and boys are key actors in gender transformation and can be obstacles or allies for gender equality. Thus, by engaging men and boys, it reduces the barriers women and girls face in building their own individual agency, address inequitable power relations, and ensures changes in power dynamics and social structures that are sustained. UNIDOR ensured that there was meticulous planning for each case to address varying needs based on age, gender, and diversity, ensuring that care arrangements were not only safe but also culturally appropriate. UNIDOR's commitment to safeguarding the physical safety and psychosocial well-being of each child underscores its dedication to humanitarian principles. The presence of a functional nutrition facility is vital for the referral, admission and treatment of eligible children under five and the PLWs.
The process started with the recruitment of nutrition staff such as the community Nutrition Volunteers, community nutrition workers, and mother to mother support groups in the targeted payams. UNIDOR conducted early nutrition screening using the mid upper arm circumference (MUAC) tap and provided preventive services such as health and nutrition education messaging, soap to caretakers to improve hygiene and address the WASH aspects as the underlining causes to malnutrition. Utilizing the MUAC tape, dedicated volunteers conducted regular screenings to assess nutritional status and identify at-risk individuals promptly. This proactive approach not only facilitated early intervention but also ensured that those in need received timely referrals to appropriate healthcare facilities. The mother-to-mother support groups played a crucial role during bi-weekly meetings. These sessions served as vital platforms for knowledge-sharing, empowerment, and collective problem-solving among caregivers as they discussed breast feeding practices such as early initiation of breast feeding, exclusive breast feeding, complementary feeding and continue feeding. The experienced mothers imparted practical advice on improving Maternal Infant and Young Child Nutrition (MIYCN) practices, fostering a nurturing environment for sustainable health improvements.
